name: Me'phaa
confidence_why: Every description from Radin 1933 and Wichmann 1992-2010 on Azoyú to Marlett & Weathers 2018 treats Me'phaa as a tone language, and Marlett & Weathers 2018, Uchihara & Tiburcio Cano 2021 and the instrumental study of Cornelio Tiburcio 2022 all put the strong syllable on the last syllable of the word, against only Herrera Zendejas 2018's claim (a phonetic survey volume) that accent follows the rightmost highest tone, which Cornelio Tiburcio 2022 tested and rejected; the one open point is whether that final prominence is phonetic stress at all, which Marlett & Weathers 2018 themselves leave undecided.
catalog_citation: Marlett, Stephen A. & Mark L. Weathers. 2018. The sounds of Me'phaa (Tlapanec): A new assessment. SIL-Mexico Electronic Working Papers 25. México: Instituto Lingüístico de Verano, A.C. 31 pp. (archive record mexico.sil.org/resources/archives/76311; genus-wide, Azoyú [tpc] sampled from Azoyú and Zapotitlán de la Fuente, Table 1 p. 4)
catalog_locator: Sec. 7 'Prominence', p. 23; Sec. 6 'Tones', pp. 22-23; Sec. 8.2 'Rhymes', p. 25
catalog_quote: It is not clear whether something comparable to stress is appropriately identified in Meꞌphaa. However, there is evidence that words and phrases are prosodically right-headed. Rensch (1978:631) refers to the “tonic ultima”. Suárez (1983:26) likewise gives reasons for considering that, at least at an earlier stage of the language, the final syllable was accented. Poser (1990) has provided ample evidence that a language (Japanese, in his case) may have foot structure despite not having a “stress system”. First, as we have alluded to already, various phonetic details require reference to a weak syllable of the root. In a disyllabic root, the final syllable is strong and the first is weak. Beyond displaying slight phonetic differences (always lenition) not observed as frequently in strong syllables, weak syllables are often the locus for more significant substitutions historically, including replacing /b/ with /w/ and /k/ with /h/, as mentioned earlier. Monosyllabic minor class words (discourse markers, subordinators) typically have the properties of weak syllables. The addition of an affix does not affect the basic prosodic structure; the root in the word continues to have a weak syllable followed by a strong one.
world_status: statement found in an open source

The closing sentence 'The addition of an affix does not affect the basic prosodic structure; the root in the word continues to have a weak syllable fo…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Me'phaa (all varieties, Azoyú included in the sample) is a tone language (High, Mid, Low with one- and two-tone melodies on roots; for Azoyú Wichmann gives 3 level + 4 contour tones, normally confined to the last two syllables of the word). The authors decline to posit stress as such but state that prosody is right-headed: the final syllable of the root is the strong syllable and preceding syllables are weak (site of lenition, k>h, b>w, d>[r], vowel shortening/loss); affixes do not shift this, so the strong syllable is root-final, which in practice is word-final since suffixes fuse with the root-final vowel and prefixes are weak. If one codes the prominence as stress it is fixed final (iambic), quantity-insensitive.
new_statements.exceptions: No word-level exceptions to final strength are given. Monosyllabic minor-class words (discourse markers, subordinators) pattern as weak syllables; in lexicalized phrases and compounds the leftward syllables reduce; some contour melodies sit on monosyllables. For Azoyú specifically the authors note only that some words keep [d] in weak syllables (incomplete d>r change, p. 9) and that Azoyú tone melodies differ from the highland varieties (p. 22).
new_statements.domain_note: Claim is made for the Me'phaa genus as a whole ('words and phrases are prosodically right-headed'); domain of the weak/strong asymmetry is the root within the word, unaffected by affixation; data are citation forms. Wichmann's Azoyú-specific work adds that phonological tone is restricted to the last two syllables of the word (Wichmann 2010, conventions, prepub p. 22), consistent with a right-edge prosodic head, but he never describes stress.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source (Marlett & Weathers 2018) is a genus-wide assessment of Me'phaa covering ISO tcf, tpc, tpl and tpx; its Azoyú [tpc] data come from the towns of Azoyú [tpc-Azoy] and Zapotitlán de la Fuente [tpc-ZFue] (speaker Constantino Zavaleta Navor), and the prominence claim is stated for Me'phaa as a whole rather than separately for Azoyú. The Azoyú-specific describer (Wichmann 1992-2010, fieldwork in Azoyú town) gives only tone facts (3 level + 4 contour tones, tone confined to the last two syllables) and never mentions stress. Cornelio Tiburcio 2022, the only instrumental stress study of Me'phaa, describes Ciénega del Sauce (mun. Ayutla de los Libres), which INALI and Marlett & Weathers treat as an Acatepec-type variety (approx. Glottolog acat1239), not Azoyú. The catalog already holds acat1239 from Marlett & Neri Remigio 2012 with the same family-level 'iambic, final syllable strong, no stress identified' note; the azoy1236 entry would rest on the same authors' 2018 genus-wide statement.

new_statements.quote: Tlapanec employs iambic feet aligned to the right edge of the prosodic word (Marlett and Weathers 2018: 23; Suárez 1983: 26). The acoustic correlate of accent in Tlapanec is still unclear. [...] Marlett and Weathers (2018: 23–24) remark that there is evidence that words and phrases are prosodically right-headed (whether this syllable has a short vowel or long vowel; thus, quantity-insensitive), since various phonological and phonetic details require reference to a weak syllable of the foot. This is also corroborated by the fact that a vowel can undergo syncope in any syllable except for this strong syllable. Some contrasts are maintained only in the final syllable of the prosodic word; this is the phonological correlate of accent.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing Marlett & Weathers 2018 statement (which it quotes and builds on): same right-headed/final placement, tone language. Adds: quantity-insensitive iambic feet built right-to-left, secondary accent on non-head feet, the prosodic word as the domain of accentuation, the phonological correlates (length/nasalization/contour tone contrasts only in the final syllable; syncope; onset requirement), and a survey of the competing acoustic-correlate hypotheses. Caveat: data are from the Huehuetepec variety, not Azoyú; the generalizations are stated as pan-Tlapanec.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tlapanec has three level tones (L, M, H; TBU = mora) and, on top of the tone, a fixed word-final prominence: the last syllable of the prosodic word is the 'strong' syllable, the head of a quantity-insensitive iambic foot aligned to the right edge of the word. Whether this prominence is phonetic stress is left open (the acoustic correlate is 'still unclear'; the authors therefore say 'weak/strong' rather than 'unstressed/stressed'), but its phonological correlates are firm: vowel length, nasalization and contour tones contrast only in the final strong syllable, syncope never hits it, and it requires an onset more strictly than weak syllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: feet are 'assigned iteratively from right to left' (p. 100), and 'the strong syllable is indicated with a raised vertical line, while secondary accent is indicated with a lowered vertical line' (p. 100); ex. (19) ni(gi.ˌta)(ʃmá.ˈtaa) 'he was pulled' shows secondary accent on the head of the non-final iamb, with the leftover initial syllable unfooted. Fn. 13: right-to-left, quantity-insensitive iambs are typologically rare.
new_statements.exceptions: Acoustic correlate disputed: Carrasco Zúñiga (2012) proposes onset-consonant duration in the strong syllable (which the authors' impression and Cornelio Tiburcio in prep. support); Herrera Zendejas (2018) instead 'claims that the accent is assigned to the syllable which has the right-most highest tone' (p. 88), not adopted. Contour tones are 'generally' limited to the final syllable 'although there are a very few cases of contour tones in non-final syllables' (p. 87). Compounded roots are not counted for footing and 'may not constitute one prosodic word' (fn. 14, p. 100). Speakers have difficulty identifying the strong syllable (p. 88).
new_statements.identity_note: The article's data are from the Huehuetepec variety (community of Zilacayotitlán; second author is a native speaker), not from Azoyú (tpc). The authors state the prosodic generalizations for Tlapanec as a whole, citing Marlett & Weathers 2018 (genus-wide, Azoyú among the sampled varieties) and Suárez 1983 (Malinaltepec). Fn. 3 notes the passive allomorphy itself may be limited to Huehuetepec; the foot/accent generalization is not so restricted in the text.

new_statements.quote: Tlapanec has been argued to employ quantity-insensitive iambic feet and aligns them at the right edge of the prosodic word, assigned iteratively from right to left (cf. Marlett and Weathers 2018). This can be illustrated by the following example. In the following, the strong syllable is indicated with a raised vertical line, while secondary accent is indicated with a lowered vertical line. (19) ni(gi.ˌta)(ʃmá.ˈtaa) ‘he was pulled’ [...] The Tlapanec prosodic word can be defined as the domain of accentuation, the domain of a minimality requirement, and the domain of some tonal processes.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement between the opened work and the catalog's existing statement (Marlett & Weathers 2018), which it cites and extends: both place prominence on the final syllable of the prosodic word and both treat the language as tonal with the phonetic status of stress uncertain. The one dissent is reported inside the source: Herrera Zendejas (2018, Mapa fónico de las lenguas mexicanas vol. 3, not opened here) claims accent falls on the syllable bearing the rightmost highest tone, i.e. tone-conditioned rather than fixed final; Uchihara & Tiburcio Cano reject this in favour of fixed final strong position with onset-consonant duration as the likely correlate (Carrasco Zúñiga 2012), and the Cornelio Tiburcio 2022 CIESAS thesis already held by the project in this folder (Ciénega del Sauce variety) confirms fixed final stress instrumentally.

sources.note: Instrumental + phonological study of an Ayutla (Acatepec-type, not Azoyú) variety: stress is fixed on the last syllable of the phonological word, quantity-insensitive iambic; the only reliable acoustic correlate is lengthening of the onset consonant of the final syllable; vowel length, nasality and contour tones contrast only in the final (tonic) syllable; tones do not affect stress position (pp. 3-4 hypotheses; pp. 171-173 conclusions). Reviews prior claims: Marlett & Weathers 2012/2018 fixed final, Carrasco 2012 ms. fixed final with onset-duration cue, Herrera Zendejas 2018 tone-conditioned.
